newsitem.title: USA: Sex accusations a never-ending story for Clinton. [CORRECTED 22:00 GMT]
newsitem.headline: Sex accusations a never-ending story for Clinton. [CORRECTED 22:00 GMT]

text.p: For the Clinton White House, it has been the nightmare that keeps coming back: yet another headline about accusations of extramarital sex involving the president.

The Supreme Court's decision on Tuesday that Paula Jones could go ahead with her sexual harassment lawsuit against Bill Clinton was only the latest in a series of news stories linking sex and the president. What one Clinton aide labeled "bimbo eruptions" during his 1992 presidential campaign have recurred at unpredictable intervals since Clinton moved into the White House.

And while First Lady Hillary Rodham Clinton declared several years ago that eventually all the stories "will wind up in the garbage can," en route to the trash bin they have become part of the lore of her husband's presidency.
Even before Clinton began running for president, he faced swirling rumours of extramarital affairs.

Before he announced his campaign in Little Rock, Arkansas late in 1991, then-Governor Clinton told interviewers he enjoyed a "zone of privacy" that would allow him to refuse to answer certain questions about his private life.
But his bid for the Democratic presidential nomination was stunned by the allegation by a former nightclub singer named Gennifer Flowers that she had had a 12-year affair with him.

Clinton and his wife went on CBS's "60 Minutes" programme to try to put the matter behind them. Clinton acknowledged "wrongdoing" and "causing pain in my marriage" but refused to respond when asked whether he had ever committed adultery.
"I think what the press has to decide is, are we going to engage in a game of gotcha?" the would-be president asked.

His campaign survived that episode, but before he had spent a year in the White House two Arkansas state troopers from Clinton's security detail told The American Spectator magazine in 1993 that they had facilitated frequent trysts for the governor with several women in Little Rock.

The White House called the charges "false and outrageous' and Clinton's defenders wondered whether the media was trying to "bring down the presidency." Clinton tried to remain above the fray, saying he was trying to keep his mind on his work.

Some six weeks later Paula Jones appeared at her first news conference to accuse Clinton of sexual misdeeds, saying the president had asked her for "a type of sex" when the two were alone in an Arkansas hotel room in 1991.
The White House denied the account and said Clinton did not know her, which officials maintain to this day.
In October 1994 Jones said she would press ahead with her lawsuit after Clinton's attorneys rejected a settlement offer. Her attorneys said Clinton could have avoided the lawsuit with an apology.

The Clinton White House appears to have won at least one public relations victory in the long battle of sexual misconduct allegations and denials. In 1996 (corrects from 1995), a former FBI agent, Gary Aldrich, published a book alleging secret, late-night assignations by the president while in the White House. White House aides denounced it as a fabrication.

But a recent article in the New Yorker magazine quoted Aldrich as saying the anecdote about Clinton ducking the Secret Service to make secret visits to a downtown Washington hotel was merely "hypothetical."
Aldrich is defending his book, but it has been widely questioned, including by some of Clinton's critics.
